utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm sorry we were delayed for a little this morning. May I remind you, Mr. Svicevic, of the affirmation you took at the commencement of your evidence which still applies. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I see Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise to my learned friend. Defence has prepared a complete document, technically correct, the same one that we presented yesterday with a couple of pages missing. And now, the missing page has been provided, both in English and in B/C/S. I made it available to my colleagues from the Prosecution last night, and I would now ask the usher kindly to distribute this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rodic. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. When my learned colleague said he made it available last night, he means last night. So we will try to work accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning. Shall I call you Dr. Svicevic, Colonel Svicevic? What is your -- what title do you use now so I don't get it wrong?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Svicevic, a couple of points I wanted to pick up from yesterday's examination, your date and place of birth, if you would be so kind, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7 January 1947, a place called Prijepolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That is in which republic, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you also clarify, are you a psychologist or a psychiatrist? Is it -- I know you went to a medical faculty, but it wasn't clear what your credential was, actually.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, I said clearly that I read philosophy at the university, majoring in clinical psychology. I got both my degrees in psychology, specialising in stress and myocardial infarction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you practice, were you a clinical psychologist with a patient-client base during the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After completing my studies, I worked in the psychiatry clinic of the medical academy. I worked in a centre for personnel selection to meet the requirements of the JNA as an expert in the area of suicide. I transferred to the General Staff in the first half of the 1980s where I dealt with cases of deaths, especially suicides. And in that capacity, I took part in international congresses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you have had a considerable amount of experience on the psychologist-patient level with dealing with trauma, with grave crisis? That is an area that you would have dealt with, as opposed to, let's say, child psychology, family counseling, that kind of...?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mainly dealt with adults because that is the natural population of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And when you were in the military, did you also run a column in Narodna Armija about your psychologist or visiting your psychologist? I'd come across something and I wanted to ask you about it and see if that was a -- I don't want to use the term, kind of a dear Abby-type scenario, if you know what that refers to, but did you have a column where people could write to you and you would respond anonymously?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was something of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And how successfully was that received by the persons in the military? Was it used?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you do some kind of work, you imply, like to believe, that there is some use in it. Otherwise you wouldn't be doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask, please, for the usher to distribute a copy of a column from Narodna Armija and ask you a little bit about how it worked, what types of responses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's in both languages. My understanding is you -- you are relatively fluent in English as well. Is that correct, Doctor? Dr. Svicevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not fluent, but I have a solid command of English. I can communicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: All right. The article that I'm looking at is on the right-hand side in the B/C/S, and the translation is the -- well, the psychologist with you is -- seems to be the name of the column. And is that your signature? Is that your name at the bottom of the column? Is this a column that you were using to assist various members of the armed services?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Radoslav Svicevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's not a second Dr. Radoslav Svicevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And this was dated 10 May 1990. The topic is one that -- kind of advice for the lovelorn, but it also has a deep -- a deeper meaning. And you -- it talks about a young man who because of his looks and inferiority complex and expressed concern to the point where he was thinking of the worst, and you gave a certain amount of advice. How many of such columns did you actually write? How many answers did you give to persons on this level? How long did this column run?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of months, I believe. But I ran such columns in many other magazines in Serbia, and this answer fits into one of my previous answers concerning my professional preferences and my specialisation in suicides. This letter reflects a crisis involving suicidal intentions, and my answer is addressed to a man who was obviously in a crisis. I believe this is a correct, professional, and human gesture on my part, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Madam Interpreter. The discretion -- at the bottom, there is kind of a little section that says that discretion is assured, everything is code named. Now, you said you also wrote in other publications. Which ones did you participate in? Which ones did you write in and where were they? Were they in Serbia or...?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in Serbia, in newspapers and publications with high circulation. It would take me some time to recollect their names. But I also wrote in professional magazines. So I wrote in publications intended for the masses, but also in professional papers. And what is added here, discretion is guaranteed, that is something that was added by the editor. I had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your works or your column was also seen in other republics, not just in Serbia. And when you were doing private writing, did it go beyond Serbia as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole territory of Yugoslavia was covered, especially in 1995 -- sorry, 1990. This issue is from 1990. At that time, it was distributed across the whole territory of Yugoslavia, not only in Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the course of your being in the command of the 2nd Operational Group, did you also find yourself in a position to offer psychological assistance to any of the troops within that composition?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How was that accomplished? Did you have -- were you offered an office or did you make the rounds and visit the units in their various posts?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three places, three clinics, most usually in the Trebinje hospital where traumatised patients who also had physical injuries would come. Another place was at the command of the 2nd Operations Group, and on a couple of occasions I went directly to visit troops in the field. Maybe it would be interesting for you to hear about these interventions in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll get back to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may ask, please, that this exhibit be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm tempted to ask of the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Background, Your Honour. I think this is part of -- this is a liaison officer who is very much a part of the public who is known, and he also has a specialty which I think is very relevant to some of the issues that are going to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, my eyes are yet to be opened. But very well. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P213.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there a trust that was built up between you and the troops?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am by nature the kind of man who tends to build such relationship with all people. And with troops, I also had a sent mental relationship because they were young men the same age as my children. And if you want me to and if we have time, I can elaborate on the topic for a long time. But I would -- I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As much as I would like to, the time becomes a factor. But thank you. Did you have any concern for the effects of the conflict on the other side? How did you view what war does to both sides?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could offer you at this moment a paper if you could accept it which would best reflect the profile --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't think we need that kind of detail. But was that something in your -- did you factor the effect of conflict also in how you, perhaps, counseled people? I mean, certainly you were in a conflict where people once worked together and now they were fighting with each other. How did you deal with that with your patients in the field?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I worked following my professional and humane ethics. But I do not understand the meaning of your question. If you would clarify it, I would be pleased to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The problems that affected the troops in the 2nd Operational Group, would you agree that the same types of problems affected the troops on the other side, affects of conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am confused by this question because in the operations group, we did not have any troops. We had a couple of soldiers who were gofers for the command of the operations group. But the area covered by the 2nd Operations Group involved troops from the 37th Corps and the 9th Naval Sector, and problems sometimes arose that called for my attention as a professional. I said yesterday that I joined the 2nd Operations Group because of psychological and social problems that arose in the field, especially in the mobilisation in the area of Nevesinje, from which these units were formed. If you mean by your question whether I had empathy for the other side, I certainly did. In addition to the fact that I am an officer, and I believe an honourable man, I'm also a good Christian. And I would not like others to suffer what I would not like inflicted on myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Svicevic. Now, I want to just confirm something. Yesterday, you indicated you were in -- under three different commanders of the operations group. You indicated Cokic, Ruzinovski, and Strugar. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mentioned a person named Sofronije Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The authority that Mr. Jeremic enjoyed that you defined on behalf of the commander of the 2nd Operational Group to make decisions, how did you work with him? Were there -- he was a liaison officer, you were a liaison officer. How were you splitting your duties, or who made that call?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the nature of things, all communications were in the 9th Naval Sector, all communications equipment was there. And whenever we wanted something sent, we had to address ourselves to Sofronije Jeremic, at least when those communications were meant for the representatives of Dubrovnik and the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who was Celebic? Could you please tell us who that person was. I believe his name may have come up.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Warship Captain Celebic, in other words a naval officer, was a member of the main inspection service of the JNA, and in that capacity he arrived with a group of others in the area of Herzegovina. And when I would leave to visit with my family, he would stand in for me in contacts with Jeremic and with representatives of Dubrovnik and the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So Jeremic was part -- Jeremic was part of the 9th VPS, and Celebic came from the inspectorate to the 2nd Operational Group specially. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there from the establishment of the 2nd Operations Group. He was part of the establishment in Belgrade as well as in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your position as liaison officer required you to have a fair amount of interface with the media and the public. Had you been aware of that at the time you were made or placed in this position, that you would have this type of exposure?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't give it much thought, but it would impose itself. I held a responsibility, and my responsibility also included the lives of others and well being of others. So yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There was a considerable amount of attention placed by the international community on the events in the Dubrovnik area. You would agree with that, I assume, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you find yourself having to make an effort and take great care in the statements you would make to the public as a result of the -- the attention that was paid on the area?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, spontaneously, conducive to my way of behaviour and with full awareness of my responsibility, that's what my conduct and behaviour was. I always tried to make it proper, and I mentioned two situations yesterday when I reacted emotionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you find yourself having to -- excuse me, let me rephrase that. The relationships that you had to establish with the European Community Monitoring Mission, ECMM, and your counterparts on the Croatian side, did you find that there was great effort that had to be exerted by you -- was there pressure for you? Was it difficult for you to reach out to these people?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't find it difficult. I didn't need to exert extra effort because communications with people was part of my profession, part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you remember a monitor fairly early on by the name of Adrien Stringer?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if we can, please, to recall -- I don't know -- it's D -- it's -- Mr. Stringer's statement was admitted into evidence by the Defence. And I'd like to make a few references to it and ask you a couple of points about some things Mr. Stringer said. D1, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There was a discussion yesterday about reaching across lines and having communication. And Mr. Stringer on page 12 of his statement has made a reference to something that he said you said. And the question about establishing direct contact with the Croatians came up. "The crisis committee said there were no problems in Cavtat and that the police are able to cope and that no military presence was required. They offer to establish direct telephone link between the JNA and the Croatian Army, but this was declined by the JNA on the grounds that the Croatian Army, ZNG, is an illegal organisation. Colonel Svicevic said that it was a 'terrorist organisation' from one party performing a genocide, fascist ideology." What would be behind those words "terrorist organisation, one party," why would that preclude your having direct communications with the other side? Would that not have been -- whatever the other side may have been in your eyes, would it not have facilitated a peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I came to The Hague, I looked at some videotapes, and I have a videocassette in my possession in Belgrade which records the contacts I had with Mr. Stringer. And within the frameworks of what was said then and what can be seen, and after all the other observations, that that meeting was conducted in a proper manner, that it was a good meeting, and that it was the start of our contacts where we can say that the principal officer performing the liaison officer was Mr. Jeremic, and also Mr. Zec, who was warship captain at the time. Now, what it says here as being part of my statement, I can accept the fact that I said that, although I don't remember having said it. The reason I said it, if I did, is that the paramilitary organisations were considered to be embodied in the Croatian National Guards Corps, and the official terminology of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia were referred to in that way, and the directive was that from these positions the opposite side, and this applied to the area of the whole of Croatia...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. The discussion yesterday to which you -- which mentioned that Mr. Van Houten did not want you to continue as a negotiator seemed to have caught you by surprise.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know or do you recall a person with whom you may have negotiated named Petar Poljanic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Poljanic, if you could remember with that, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the representative of Dubrovnik, but I didn't contact with him much. Djuro Kolic was the principle negotiator, but Mr. Poljanic, Mr. Obuljen but Mr. Poljanic from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you dealt with Mr. Kolic as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly with Kolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask, please, to have distributed by the usher an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Doctor, you have in front of you -- do you have a -- you have it in front of you? Dr. Svicevic, is it --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is a fax that was sent by Mr. Poljanic as the president of the municipal assembly of Dubrovnik. It was sent to General Strugar and to the ECMM on the 7th of November 1991 indicating that "representatives of our municipality who are involved in talks in Cavtat with representatives of the JNA in the presence of the European mission representatives in an effort to find peaceful solutions to the present situation and avoid further loss of life and the destruction of property have complained several times about the way in which the talks are being handled by your representative, Lieutenant Colonel Radoslav Svicevic, who they say is constantly obstructing any attempts to find any kind of practical solution to problems faced by the civilian population, especially those relating to the repair of water and electricity networks and supply. This person is constantly airing his political views which makes the talks difficult, although at the same time he emphasises that political issues should be solved at other higher levels. According to their latest report, the behaviour of Mr. Svicevic at the meeting of 6 November 1991 escalated beyond all bounds. He directly obstructed efforts to reach an agreement on solutions that had been on the agenda for weeks and rudely insulted our representative, Mr. Djuro Kolic by crassly comparing him to the war criminal Artukovic. In order to restore normal communication, I am taking the liberty of asking you to appoint along with Mr. Svicevic or instead of him an officer of higher rank who will have a constructive approach to resolving the humanitarian issues advocated by the representatives of the European Community Monitoring Mission." Were you called into the command of the 2nd Operational Group any time after the 7th of November to discuss this letter or the contents of this letter?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a regular basis daily, depending on the needs, of course, and what was on the agenda, I would go to the command of the 2nd Operational Group for meetings, and at times they were with General Strugar, too. So -- but actually, this is the first time I see this document. I don't know -- I'm not aware of a document with this content coming into the operational group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question that my learned colleague posed is improper because as we can see from the document it wasn't sent to the 2nd Operational Group, but to the VPS of Boka. That is, the naval sector of Boka. So that is quite clear and says so in line 1 and line 2. It says "send to the Boka VPS," and then it says later on "to Boka VPS command." It says that in two places. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there is an objection on the floor, I don't know how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The objection is noted. But I also notice it's addressed to General Strugar. So if you would carry on with your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My question was: Did General Strugar discuss the content of this letter with you at a point after the 7th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite obviously we did not discuss this because had we discussed this letter, it would have been shown me. This is the first time I see this letter. But if I may be allowed to explain or comment in a few words.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell me, were you aware of the fact that Mr. Poljanic and Mr. Kolic objected to how you were conducting yourself and its -- the effect of your conduct on negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in one situation, and that was when I said that there were two incidents. I meant one -- may I be allowed to explain, one that is mentioned here with respect to Artukovic and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just tell us, who is Artukovic for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May we take this in sequence, please. May I be allowed to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I want to get the questions answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you allow the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this conduct is essential and is very important to me, so would you please allow me to answer because this touches upon my moral integrity, in a way. At one point in this document, it says that Svicevic stresses that political questions should be solved at another higher level. And that is how it was. We dealt with general issues related to the Dubrovnik region, whereas they went on to politicise all the problems that occurred. And I stressed that political issues should be solved at other higher levels, which meant that we dealt with humanitarian issues. Now, who was Artukovic? That is that second incident that I wanted to raise with respect to my sojourn in the area. Mr. Kolic during our talks would very often stress that his mother was a Serb. And I remember a meeting when another incident took place where some people had a fallen casualty, and I said that Andrea Artukovic's mother was a Serb, too, and Andrea Artukovic was a well-known Ustasha criminal, and that is he worked in the official ideology during World War II, the Ustasha movement, and he was characterised as such. So an incident did arise with respect to that. And at another meeting, because of the fact that Mr. Djuro Kolic thought that I said something against him, I apologised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask that this exhibit be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask that this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence objects to the introduction of this document. Because the witness says he never saw this document, he has not identified it in any way, the document is not signed, it is an unknown source, unknown origins, so there are no grounds that have been laid for this document to be entered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is fully familiar with the content of the document, has commented on it, knows who the authors of the document is, and it is highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P214.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Doctor, you also in the course of your duties have been quoted considerably in the media, and I wanted to ask you a few points about some of the quotes where your name has appeared in the media, both within areas in Yugoslavia and outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I could ask, please, to distribute this document. I regret that there is no translation, but I believe that -- it is a small article, and the interpreters have it, and I believe I can ask you for your assistance, Doctor. It would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What is before you, if you would be kind enough to read the title of it. It says "war chronicle," but if you would give us a hand it would be very helpful. Are you able to do that, Doctor, where it says Ratna Hronika?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough just to read it to us in your language and it will be picked up by the interpreting section.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want the whole text?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... title part, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what newspaper is this? What article? Where does it come from? When? I really don't understand the course that the cross-examination is taking. What newspaper is this from? What is the date? I can't see anything here in addition to the fact that we don't have the translation. But that's of lesser importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Please allow me if I may to inquire of the doctor if he's familiar with this particular publication.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Have you seen this publication before in any of its forms?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then just for purposes of perhaps taking a look -- in the middle of it where it says 7/11/91. 7/11/91, now this is whether or not we seek to admit it, I just want to ask a question of it. It happens to discuss wartime events, and on the 11 -- it cites for November 11th a comment that is attributable to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this manner of cross-examination. The witness has not seen the document. We do not know from which newspaper the document is taken. All we have is a piece of paper in front of us, and on the basis of that piece of paper the witness is being asked questions. I really don't understand what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to just ask if the comment that is in there is attributable, is correctly attributable to him, and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might ask the witness to read it and ask whether the comment is correctly attributable to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Will do. That is what my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Without him reading it aloud at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Without him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to take a look at what is in the -- do you see, Doctor, I'll point it to you, where it says 7/11/91.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true that I could have said this, "a schizophrenic Mesic." I certainly could not have said that, and did not say it, refer to Mesic as being schizophrenic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I could ask for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Doctor, this is the text of an article from 25th October 1991 out of -- the author of the article is a Marcus Tanner. And the title of it is "Federal army tightens siege of Dubrovnik." It is from The Independent, and this is a summary of the article. There is a -- about in the middle of the page, "federal army leaders in Zagreb yesterday denied shelling the historic Old Town. A local army commander, Colonel Radoslav Svicevic, also dismissed Croatian claims that army artillery damaged parts of the Old Town as `lies and fabrication'. Captain Milan Zec commanding of frigate at nearby Plato said that the army had specific orders not to damage the Old Town area and accused the Croats of detonating several buildings in Dubrovnik themselves as part of a 'diabolical fascist plan to destroy the Old Town and then blame the Yugoslav Army.'" In October of 1991, what did you know about any allegations from your contacts either with the media, the ECMM, other foreign dignitaries or international organisations, or your own units about the alleged shelling by the JNA of the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this document makes no sense because it says "local army commander Radoslav Svicevic." I never was a local army commander, and I don't think this deserves any further comment. However, I will answer your questions. At that time, there was a second round of rumours about great damage inflicted on Dubrovnik. According to all the information and intelligence that we gathered through the 2nd Operations Group and other sources, we could not see that there was any damage to Dubrovnik, at least not the kind of damage that they seemed to emphasise. And that was one of the reasons why a visit was organised by journalists and ambassadors to Dubrovnik. So the initiative for that visit and tour of Dubrovnik which followed on the 28th of October, and that is after this, came directly from the command of the 2nd Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you yourself visit Dubrovnik during that period of time to confirm whether or not there was damage? When I say "Dubrovnik," I mean the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As agreed with Frigate Captain Sofronije Jeremic, it was he who accompanied the group because he was a naval officer and knew the town very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you think that the claims were exaggerated so that you would be quoted as suggesting that the damage was lies and fabrication? Did you believe it was exaggerated or not true?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say there were lies or fabrications. I said according to all the information available to us, that's what I said, there was no such thing. Maybe you could say we did not have enough information, but according to all the information we had, there was no shelling of Dubrovnik. And finally, after this tour by journalists and ambassadors, it was noted that a small house in Radzura Boskovica Street was damaged, and media representatives analysed this damage and commented upon it. And from all that analysis, it seemed to follow that this projectile could not have come either from the sea or from land, although of course I'm not a ballistic expert. I hope I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So after the, as it were, inquiry by the public or by the media, you addressed the issue, and you were misquoted. Is that what you're suggesting, that you were misquoted, but that you did comment about the allegations of damage from shelling by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said I emphasised that according to our information, there was no such damage. I insisted on that. And that is also why I insisted together with General -- with Colonel Strugar that this tour of Dubrovnik be organised for journalists. And indeed, shortly a group of 40 reporters toured Dubrovnik. There was one reporter from Associated Press who made photos and noted that there was light damage, saying as well that he couldn't tell how it was inflicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask, please, to move this article in to evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you mean 215?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is not an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is P215.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you, Madam Usher, please distribute an article that again we regret that we were unable under time constraints to get a translation, but the portions I think you'll be able to assist us with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As with the Defence when they were in the similar position, you will provide translations in due course if these are translated -- if these are received?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Svicevic, I have in Serbo-Croatian basically two pages, one of which has smaller print and it is the complete article. And the other one is a bit enlarged so that the area of emphasis is easier to read. But it is a copy of an article from Politika from 25 October 1991. It is a -- the title of it is "old Dubrovnik was not bombed, shelled, bombed. Where is Politika from? What type of publication -- where does it hail from? Where is it based out of?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very reputable Serbian-Belgrade newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the article -- sorry, I will actually hold it up so that -- it's a little difficult, but I have yellowed it so you can perhaps direct the Chamber's attention to the area I'm looking at, it's yellowed, in the larger text and also to my learned colleagues opposite, and also to you, Doctor, I'm going to ask you about a quote in there, if I may. It's over on the -- as you look at the article, if you look at the bigger print, the right-hand side -- could I ask you just to look up for a second and I'll show you where I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is the bigger print. If you could be good enough to assist us -- first of all, was I correct in the title of the article? What is it entitled, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a newspaper headline. Newspaper headline written by a journalist, I stress. "Old Dubrovnik was not shelled."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And above it, there's a little kind of a byline above it. What does that say, please, if you would be kind enough?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Representatives of this town implore" --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This area right here.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From the Dubrovnik front line."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could just give us then -- underneath the title, if you would be good enough to read what it says. I'd stop and see -- you started to do it.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Representatives of this town implore that fire be ceased. JNA does not accept a cease-fire, demanding instead that paramilitaries lay down their arms. After a land attack, there followed a naval assault on Kupari and landing, after which this place was taken hold of by the JNA. Five killed and 22 JNA members wounded."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you look at the area that I have yellowed, and I'll show you again, over on the right hand, there is a -- your name is mentioned. Could you read the sentence in which your name is mentioned, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Lieutenant Colonel Telebak [phoen]" --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It's a fabrication that the JNA fired even a single shell on Dubrovnik. Lieutenant Colonel Radoslav Svicevic and Frigate Captain Milan Zec said the same. Commanding officer Milan Zec, whom he found at the position close to Dubrovnik, does not rule out the possibility there were explosions in Old Town of Dubrovnik, but he fears that he might be a beginning of that terrible plan of Tudjman's mercenaries to blow the whole ancient town up because JNA units are coming closer and closer to Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the date of this article, if you could confirm it, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is -- you have described this as a reputable newspaper. In your view, this is a reputable newspaper.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time -- I just wish to add, it was also the official the government newspaper. The official government medium.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Government of?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the authorities of Yugoslavia. At that time, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. May I again request that it be assigned an exhibit number and move into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The translation into English noted its date as the 24th of August -- of October. Is it not the 25th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is, sir, the 25th. I didn't catch that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P216.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Svicevic, you have indicated you're aware or you were aware at the time of the concern raised over the allegations of shelling by the JNA of the Old Town area so much so that news -- that the media was invited to go and see. Are you able to indicate to us what if any disciplinary inquiries, punishment, may have been meted out as a result of the -- well, perhaps let's just ask what inquiries internally are you aware of that may have been initiated as a result of these allegations? Do you know of any?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, during examination-in-chief, there was a discussion about some correspondence or about allegations that were raised from a 4 November 1991 communication to Admiral Brovet from General Strugar. Do you recall there was a discussion about some allegations about gases and hotels and ECMM monitors' allegations, and I believe you said that a monitor was removed as a result of this particular incident. Do you remember discussing that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember yesterday's discussion. But your question doesn't really tell me anything now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How -- do you know how that set of allegations got to the attention of Admiral Brovet so that General Strugar had to respond? How did he become -- how did Brovet become aware of it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I can give you a guess, but that was at the level of a superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask, please, just to recall for a moment D50, D-5-0.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Doctor, this exhibit was introduced by the Defence. That's why it has a D as part of its numbering. And it is a communication to a Colonel Lukic, Lieutenant Svicevic, inform the general and act in accordance to his decision. Urgently -- it is from Admiral Brovet. "Urgently deliver the information regarding the allegations from the protest of the international monitoring mission, EC, from the 3/11/1991" -- it's a bit loosely translated, sorry. But you yourself did not transmit these allegations to General Strugar? They had to come from Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they did not come to me directly from Admiral Brovet. It had to follow the chain of command. I have had to receive it from General Strugar or his assistants, Stankovic or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was another name the interpreter didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Or ECMM went directly to Admiral Brovet because they did not get any response locally?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, regarding interpretation, just one thing: A part of the sentence is not on record where he said that he had no direct communication with the superior command. That is, with Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I see that there is -- let me just confirm. I don't know which name may be have refer -- have been referred to, but Lukic, Svicevic, I'm not sure, if there's a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was your response that had a name that was not picked up by the interpreter. Could you think back to what your answer was. You said Stankovic or -- you had said or "I have had to receive it from" -- yeah. What would that be.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Damjanovic or Stankovic, his close associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General Strugar --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here again, Your Honours, and I'm sorry, Mrs. Somers, to interpret you. The whole sentence that followed this one that my learned friend is discussing with the witness is witness: "Namely, that Mr. Svicevic had no direct communication with Admiral Brovet whatsoever." That is the sentence that is missing and was uttered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have that now in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you're suggesting that it would have gone up the chain and back, this letter does not bear that out. It appears to have missed the chain, gone to the top and was sent back. Can you explain why that would happen with so many high-ranking officers to have been there to have responded to an ECMM complaint?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the signature Colonel Lukic and Lieutenant Colonel Svicevic? Is that what you mean? Because I don't see any other reference to my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No. What I'm suggesting is "urgently deliver the information regarding the allegations from the protest of the international monitoring mission." Why does that come from Admiral Brovet, who is by all accounts a superior officer, commander, commander to the 2nd Operational Group? Why is it not originating through the structured interaction of the 2nd Operational Group and the European Community? Why was it not relayed to your commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, is this an integral part of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There is a request to make sure to deliver information. Why --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]....

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this came precisely through regular channels designated for communication. It came to the operations group. And the person in charge, I cannot identify this signature, forwarded it to me. So this document came from Admiral Brovet, to the 2nd Operations Group, and according to the nature of things, what follows is that the persons are identified within the 2nd Operations Group to report on the matter. Colonel Lukic was designated as assistant to the commander, so I don't see any breach of hierarchy. It is precisely an illustration of adequate hierarchy in a relationship between the superior commander and assistants within the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will ask to recall a document in one second that perhaps will assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point of your question has escaped the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think perhaps if I show him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I show him a document, it will probably make it a bit easier to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we just do it directly?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We can try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were the liaison officer between the command of the 2nd Operational Group and the monitoring mission in and around Dubrovnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you receive the document of protest or complaint from that monitoring mission yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Protests were channelled through the Military Naval Sector. And if there was any dissatisfaction or protests which occurs sometimes in the course of negotiation, superiors from the European Community addressed it to the General Staff. All these are possibilities. However, I personally did not receive any protest addressed to me, nor was it possible to send anything directly to me because, after all, in an organised army there is an organised way of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were unaware of the allegations by ECMM monitor Luke Daras about the hotels, that you had no knowledge of those allegations by the JN --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend is confusing the witness. She should point out which document she is referring to and show the witness the document so that he is able to provide an adequate answer. At this moment, he is not clear on which document he's supposed to answer. My --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I think it will be helpful for just a moment to pull back P104, and please show it to the witness. We will do this quickly before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break at about a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Svicevic, what you have been shown is an exhibit that is directed to Admiral Brovet from General Strugar dated 4 November 1991. And it is following the document you just looked at that we were discussing from the 3rd of November. And do you see the incidents that are referred to, allegations that the general is responding to point by point to Admiral Brovet? This is what the subject was, and some of it was discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I participated in the drafting of this document, and of course I am familiar with everything that is written.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you participated in the drafting of the document, are you claiming you were unaware of the facts that are alleged in the document? Are you saying that you didn't know about the allegations raised by the Croatian side that are the subject matter of this document that had to go to Admiral Brovet at his request?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean whether I was -- if I was aware or not? I could only have been informed as opposed to going somewhere to see with my own eyes. Knowledge is one thing, and information is another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... By whom?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the European Community, representatives of the European Community, and I say that they objected. And I say that. So I interpret matters correctly here. My knowledge does not imply in this case any conviction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am just the transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When were you informed of the allegations? When were you told of this --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through our regular contacts, and this is a summary of the characteristic contacts, not all of them. And something that ought to correspond to the demand sent by the General Staff as to about how an information should be sent out. And this is one case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you notify General Strugar of these allegations from the Croatian side transmitted through the European Union?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the reporting, that was regular, and it followed the report of the operational group sent out to the General Staff. Everything that was of interest from each of the meetings would be reported on, both by me and by members of the other operational group at our two-day reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And it took prompting from Admiral Brovet to get a response?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is improper.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's improper because or incorrect because I indicated to you that the communication went through regular channels. Admiral Brovet, General Strugar, General Strugar to his assistant, and then down to me. So there is no reason, and I apologise for having to say that, for you to -- well, let's avoid any unnecessary terms. But there's no need for you to tell me that I had to be encouraged by Brovet to do that. This is the normal channel of communication in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is Admiral Brovet based? Where was he at the time based?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade at the General Staff. I think he was the number-two man after General Kadijevic, in fact. I beg your pardon, Adzic, it was Adzic who was chief of the General Staff. So Brovet -- the second man, so Brovet was number three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask, please, to have the usher distribute a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with the -- these bulletins from the federal secretariat, this type of publication? Have you seen this before, the type of publication, not necessarily this one?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see this for the first time. This form of bulletin. Not the contents, but the form.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware that the federal secretariat puts out bulletins?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only assume that this was for the purposes of some narrow circle of commanders or the commanders of units on the territory of the former Yugoslavia who received this kind of bulletin because the nature of this kind of bulletin in my opinion, and I see no markings of confidentiality or anything like that, but I do think it contains certain elements of a confidential nature because I see the commander of the Novi Sad Corps was mentioned and everything that went on in Yugoslavia during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is dated -- this is from Belgrade, 5th of November 1991. And I would turn your attention to page 6, please, in the B/C/S. Is there a corresponding translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We will promise the Chamber a translation if the document is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Page 6 of the B/C/S where you are -- there is a reference to you. Would you be good enough, please, to read out what it says about Lieutenant Colonel Svicevic.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Svicevic launched energetic protests because of the observations made by members of the European mission, member Luke Daras, who said to the BBC arbitrarily that on the 2nd of November in Dubrovnik two hotels were hit."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting my learned friend, but the document that was provided to the witness is incomplete, and this can be easily seen because we have pages 3 and 4, no page 5, so the context of what she is asking is completely lost. In the lower right-hand corner we see the number of the page, and on page 6 we see the continuation of the text that was on page 5, which we do not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A valid point, Mr. Petrovic. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is -- apparently, this is what was provided from the source. The ERNs are consecutive. I will limit my comments so it does not taking anything out of context, and I accept there appears to be potentially a page that was not turned over. Might have been blank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it's hardly blank --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- if you look at the content.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm saying that I don't have a previous page. I understand that, Your Honour. But I don't have a previous page that matches up, and for some reason the ERN indicates this is what we had as a consecutive series. If the Chamber would permit me simply to inquire whether or not the date, 2nd of November, as is reflected, which is what I'm interested in asking about, is correct. And that would be the extent of the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission -- thank you. On page 4 of the document you have before you, you can see that we have the beginning of something that is not continued on page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the ERN numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact that the ERN numbers follow on from one another doesn't mean a thing because we can't see the context. We can't see what part this particular paragraph refers to, the paragraph highlighted by my learned friend. Is it a letter, a report, a comment? We know nothing about that, what it's all about. And I don't think that she should therefore ask anything about that because we can't see what this belongs to. As you can see, the document, for example, on page 2, is composed of some reports dated the 4th of November, then page 2, once again we have a letter by the federal secretary for national defence, but what it's about we don't know. On page 6, we have a mention of another report, newspaper article. Now, what the second paragraph that was quoted from paragraph [as interpreted] 6 refers to, we are not able to see. So I don't think that we can ask questions on this. It leads to general confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we just put the bulletin down and not even look at the bulletin, and may I just ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Go right ahead, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On November 2nd, is that the date where allegedly two hotels were shelled by the JNA? Was it referring to November 2nd? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned yesterday something linked to Luka Daras, and that was my protest with respect to the officers captured and one of his statements to the effect that on that day just one dog was killed in Dubrovnik. So I think that was taken out of context. It should be contained in this bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know -- are you familiar with an officer who is part of the 2nd Operational Group in the Dubrovnik area named Gojko Djurasic? Do you know him? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he has just testified here. He was the commander of Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, he was able to establish a direct contact with members of the Croatian side on issues of great importance to his, meaning Djurasic's area of -- zone of responsibility. Did you ever go up to that area to see how the -- I'm sorry, yes, go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mokosica on two or three occasions, negotiations were held with representatives of Dubrovnik and the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to see how things were working between the Croatians and I believe it was Colonel Djurasic's command there?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we had, it took place within the frameworks of the basic agreements reached and regulated with Mr. Kouchner and representatives of the Dubrovnik authorities. That means that life in Mokosica for the most part functioned normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be able to confirm that there was a constructive relationship between Colonel Djurasic and the Croatian side to facilitate the -- the situation you just described in Mokosica?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I myself was not informed about any protest from the representatives of Dubrovnik or the European Community linked to Mokosica at that time when the commander of Mokosica was Mr. Djurasic, I can only assume -- or rather, I can state that everything was in order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to be going into another area. If we're going to break in a few minutes, shall we -- shall I start it or shall I just wait for the time after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I ask you of you a time indication.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: About one more hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break now, I think, and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would ask the usher to please distribute -- I'm going to wind up. I found one or two other points that I wanted to get before I transition, and then I'll move on. Your Honours, I have been informed that the witness has to actually be out of here relatively -- well, by 1.00. I just wanted the Chamber to know there is time limitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't forget that there is re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I understand. That's why I'm -- so any -- what I'm saying is that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just move on, quickly, don't explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you understand. Got you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Doctor, because of your factors, I'm going to ask you to try to be brief in your responses, and I'll try to be very direct in my questions. I'm showing you a document from ECMM dated 6 November 1991. It is a daily report. You dealt with the ECMM regularly, did you not? Regularly?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Trebinje within the operations group, yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And just if you turn the page to page 2, this document also discusses matters such as the 11 points, the 11 points. Do you see the reference? I'm looking at the English. I didn't -- I don't think it will be page 2 necessarily in the Serbo-Croatian. If you look at the second page in English where it says page 2, see, about four lines -- five lines from the top, it makes reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be of assistance. It is at the end of the B/C/S, and that will facilitate this for the witness. So if you follow the Serbian version, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you about the 11 points is that these are matters, are they not, that were discussed between yourself and the ECMM? This is a regular type of report that would come from ECMM. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a regular report because I don't know who it was addressed to. Perhaps Split and Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at page 3, could you turn over in the English page 3, please, English. At the bottom of page 3 in English, it says "EC monitors during the discussions made at least four alternative proposals, all of them rejected by the JNA, in particular, providing JNA -- in particular, providing a JNA liaison officer in Dubrovnik and accepting a Croatian liaison officer behind their lines." What was your view on the idea of putting a JNA officer Croatian -- behind Croatian lines; and then the reverse, a Croatian officer behind JNA lines? How did you view that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a very constructive proposal, and this was followed by the fact that the European monitors ought to be on our side, too, and I mentioned that position of mine yesterday, I believe, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At the very last page in English, there is a reference to you. It's a bit difficult to read. My apologies for the copy quality. It begins actually on the bottom of the page before it, and it says: "According to our sources, the JNA representative warned us according to our sources, JNA sources, one of your members might be killed by Croatian terrorists in order to arrest the JNA -- I think it's arrest the JNA in the eyes of the world. He added that 3.000 armed people/Ustasha fascists are in the centre of Dubrovnik, but EC monitors seem not to know it. The Croatian side protested against this -- against this insult. They will request the replacement of Lieutenant Colonel Svicevic as negotiator." It is signed by various members of the EC. Can you indicate whether or not as of the 6th of December the European Union monitors addressed the concerns of the Croatians about you continued status as negotiator to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we mean the 6th of November rather than December?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, absolutely right. November.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Doctor. I meant -- I'll rephrase it for you. I'm awfully sorry. Can you indicate whether or not as of the 6th of November the European Union monitors addressed the concern of Croatia's as to your continued status as a negotiator?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly this was just the result of the incident with Mr. Kolic. However, I must say that I never had from the General Staff any criticism addressed at my -- at me for my behaviour and my work. And had there been any need for criticism, for criticising my work, the General Staff could at all times withdraw me from my post, and I would have been very happy for that to have happened. But, of course, time does not allow us to go into the details. This went Dubrovnik. The team was set up. And we objected and asked that the representatives of the European Community come in. And as the people of Dubrovnik were their hosts, they had more contacts and could have served up more information to them. So I don't want to question the credibility of the European Community or undermine it in any way. All I want to say is they could have added on to their information which was sometimes improper. They could have been briefed more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated in your answer just now the General Staff did not level any criticism. Did General Strugar level any criticism towards you about the allegations from the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because General Strugar had direct contacts with the General Staff, and quite certainly any criticisms or shortcomings on my part, if he had received orders to act upon them, would have been implemented. I would have been reprimanded or replaced or something of that kind. But this is part of the conversations we had. We defended our interests. We defended our principles --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to cut you off, but because of your time constraints and your flight I want to move on, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask that this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see no grounds for the document of one negotiating side not seen by the witness, and the witness is not able to state anything about this. He's never seen it and had it in his hands or has any connection to it that it can be introduced through this witness. I don't think that stands. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is it going to add to the record we already have, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's -- it's an indication of the sequence of complaints, Your Honour. I think it is relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But you have that recorded in the transcript from your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So what's the tender going to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It can assist in other points that indicate the interaction between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you're wanting it in to deal with other matters, that is a further reason for Mr. Petrovic to object and a further basis upon which it will not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that it is sufficient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that is the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to ask you to recall, please, Madam Usher, P61 slash -- excuse me. I think it's 28. 61-28, tab 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could I ask that it be put on the ELMO, please. Is it from the -- excuse me. Yes. Would you be good enough to put it on the ELMO, please. Thank you. This memorandum cites a number of conditions that were accepted in order to effect the return of the monitors to the Dubrovnik area after their departure in November following a number of events. Now, I want to just ask you, who was Bernard Kouchner by title? What was his -- what was his title, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a well-known personage within the Medicins San Frontieres organisation. I think he was the direct representative of the European Community, and De Mistura along with Minister Kouchner as a representative of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Van Houten was a very high-ranking member of the European Community, the head of the mission. Correct? Both very high-ranking European officials. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had contacts with the European Community coming in to the territory of the 2nd Operational Group, so I really can't comment further on the hierarchy of the EC on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. I can't address that. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you view the allegation about threats against monitors as one that was seriously considered by the ECMM people as well as the internationals generally? What was your view of it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our contacts, there was never the fear that they said that something could happen from our part. We did everything to ensure their security and safety when they came to our side because we were always afraid that some incident might not break out which would act to the disadvantage of our own side. So we couldn't have even envisaged threats at all let alone having them carried out because I was well aware of what this would all mean in the long term.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were shown yesterday the letter from Mr. Van Houten to Mr. Kouchner indicating that you were deemed not to be an acceptable negotiating partner. Now, if you look at the document in front of you, among the various conditions that are put to enable the ECMM to return, the first condition is that "people who threaten monitors are not suitable partners in negotiations and should be excluded from all negotiations while monitors are to be present." The second condition: "Written guarantees concerning the security of monitors from both parties shall be given beforehand by parties involved and local commanders and authorities. Under no circumstances are they, or the locations where they are staying or operating to be fired upon or otherwise threatened." The reference to "threatening monitors" was the very first point in a series of points to be agreed upon. After the 25th of November, how much were you allowed to participate in the negotiating process? Did you continue with the negotiating process?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I was part of the negotiations until the day, maybe the 7th or maybe the 2nd when there was a crisis. It could have been the 6th. On the 7th and 8th, I was in Belgrade. After that visit to Belgrade, I returned. And I have notes to attest to that in my working notebook. First of all, I didn't see this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... You did participate --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And this document bears a place for the endorsement of General Damjanovic from the command of the 2nd Operational Group. If you look toward the back of the document, you will note that, that there is a place for his signature. Do you see?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- yes, I see that. But I don't know on what basis I'm supposed to believe this document authentic. I don't see any signatures here. And what attracted my attention here is that Mr. Kouchner is in the last position here, whereas according to the nature of things he should be first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did General Damjanovic ever tell you you are not to participate further in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did General Strugar ever tell you you are no longer to participate in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In army, there are orders. I would have received an order not to participate in negotiations any longer. There can be no compromises in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Turning to some comments you made yesterday about the 5th of December, you indicated that there were daily meetings in the 2nd Operational Group. Now -- and I think 1800 was the time you referred. Was that general time for the daily meeting in the 2nd Operational Group or does it vary?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been an hour before or after until a member of the team from the field would arrive or an assistant of the commander in case the commander was busy elsewhere. So if you allow for this possibility, the delay could have been one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, on the 5th of December, was General Strugar present at the daily meeting which I think you put at 6 -- at 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who else was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual team of the 2nd Operational Group that was located in Trebinje at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You yourself as a negotiator know that normally -- well, you know the importance of being sure that cease-fires are adhered to. Did General Strugar at that meeting discuss the cease-fire and the negotiations that had been negotiated that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
